case_name: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala
core_issue: Basic Structure Doctrine
holding: Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution
principles_established: Basic structure doctrine
Judicial review of constitutional amendments
Parliament's amending power is not unlimited
relevance: Defines the limits of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution

case_name: Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India
core_issue: Right to life and personal liberty under Article 21
holding: Article 21 is not merely a procedure against deprivation of life and liberty but must be fair, just and reasonable
principles_established: Article 21 cannot be suspended even during emergency
Procedure established by law must be just, fair and reasonable
Golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21
relevance: Expanded the scope of Article 21 to include due process requirements

case_name: K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India
core_issue: Right to privacy as a fundamental right
holding: Right to privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution
principles_established: Right to privacy is intrinsic to life and liberty
Privacy includes informational, bodily and decisional autonomy
Overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy
relevance: Established privacy as a constitutionally protected fundamental right

case_name: S.R. Bommai vs. Union of India
core_issue: President's rule and federalism under Article 356
holding: President's power under Article 356 is subject to judicial review; secularism is part of basic structure
principles_established: Federalism and secularism are part of the basic structure
President's satisfaction under Art. 356 is justiciable
State assemblies cannot be dissolved until proclamation is approved by Parliament
relevance: Limited the arbitrary use of Article 356 to dismiss state governments

case_name: A.D.M. Jabalpur vs. Shivkant Shukla
core_issue: Writ of habeas corpus during national emergency
holding: No person has locus standi to file a habeas corpus petition during emergency when fundamental rights are suspended
principles_established: Later overruled by Puttaswamy — right to life cannot be suspended
Dissent by Justice H.R. Khanna became landmark
relevance: Controversial judgment denying habeas corpus during Emergency; subsequently overruled

case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi vs. Raj Narain
core_issue: Validity of election laws and constitutional amendments
holding: Election disputes must be decided by an independent judiciary; amendments that destroy basic structure are invalid
principles_established: Democracy and rule of law are part of basic structure
Parliament cannot validate an invalid election by constitutional amendment
Even a unanimous vote cannot override fundamental rights
relevance: Struck down Article 329A which sought to immunize Prime Minister's election from judicial scrutiny

case_name: Minerva Mills vs. Union of India
core_issue: Limits on Parliament's power to amend the Constitution
holding: Parliament cannot abrogate fundamental rights through amendment; the harmony between fundamental rights and directive principles is part of basic structure
principles_established: Limited amending power of Parliament under Art. 368
Judicial review of constitutional amendments
Fundamental rights cannot be abrogated
relevance: Struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that gave unlimited amending power to Parliament

case_name: D.K. Basu vs. State of West Bengal
core_issue: Arrest procedure and custodial violence
holding: Laid down detailed guidelines to be followed during arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence
principles_established: Right to know grounds of arrest
Right to inform family member about arrest
Right to legal representation
Right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours
Compensation for custodial death
relevance: Foundational guidelines to prevent custodial torture and protect dignity of arrested persons

case_name: Lalita Kumari vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
core_issue: Whether police can conduct preliminary inquiry before registering FIR for cognizable offences
holding: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC for cognizable offences; preliminary inquiry only in limited exceptional cases
principles_established: FIR registration is mandatory for cognizable offences
Preliminary inquiry permitted only in matrimonial/medical corruption cases
Time limit of 7 days for preliminary inquiry
relevance: Ended discretion of police to avoid registering FIRs in cognizable offences

case_name: Arnesh Kumar vs. State of Bihar
core_issue: Automatic arrest for offences punishable up to 7 years
holding: Arrest is not mandatory for offences punishable up to 7 years; police must comply with Section 41 CrPC guidelines
principles_established: No automatic arrest for offences up to 7 years imprisonment
Police must record reasons for arrest
Magistrates must not mechanically authorize detention
Anti-dowry laws should not be abused
relevance: Checked arbitrary arrests in matrimonial disputes and other offences punishable up to 7 years

case_name: State of Punjab vs. Baldev Singh
core_issue: Compliance with search procedures under NDPS Act
holding: Non-compliance with mandatory search and seizure provisions under NDPS Act renders the trial vitiated
principles_established: Right of accused to be informed of right to search before a gazetted officer or magistrate
Non-compliance with procedural safeguards vitiates conviction
Strict compliance required for NDPS searches
relevance: Protected accused persons from arbitrary searches and seizures under strict NDPS laws

case_name: Nandini Satpathy vs. P.L. Dani
core_issue: Right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3)
holding: Article 20(3) protects accused persons from being compelled to be witnesses against themselves; applies to police interrogation
principles_established: Compelled testimony includes oral as well as documentary evidence
Right against self-incrimination extends to the stage of police interrogation
Police cannot compel answers that may incriminate
relevance: Broad interpretation of the right against self-incrimination during investigation

case_name: Hussainara Khatoon vs. State of Bihar
core_issue: Right to speedy trial and undertrial prisoners
holding: Right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21; undertrial prisoners must be released if trial cannot be completed within reasonable time
principles_established: Speedy trial is an integral part of Article 21
Poverty cannot be a reason for pre-trial detention
Free legal aid is a fundamental right
relevance: Led to release of thousands of undertrial prisoners and established right to speedy trial

case_name: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab
core_issue: Constitutional validity of death penalty
holding: Death penalty is constitutional but only in the 'rarest of rare' cases
principles_established: Rarest of rare doctrine for death penalty
Death sentence must be an exception, not the rule
Aggravating and mitigating circumstances must be weighed
relevance: The guiding precedent for all death penalty sentencing in India

case_name: Selvi vs. State of Karnataka
core_issue: Constitutionality of narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests
holding: Forcible administration of narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests violates Article 20(3) right against self-incrimination
principles_established: Narcoanalysis violates right against self-incrimination
Results of such tests are not admissible as evidence
Consent-based tests are permissible with procedural safeguards
relevance: Prohibited invasive forensic interrogation techniques as violative of fundamental rights

case_name: Nikesh Tarachand Shah vs. Union of India
core_issue: Constitutional validity of stringent bail provisions under PMLA
holding: Section 45 of PMLA (twin conditions for bail) struck down as violative of Articles 14 and 21
acts_affected: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Sec. 45
principles_established: Bail conditions must not be arbitrary or disproportionate
Presumption of innocence cannot be reversed for economic offences
Twin conditions for bail violated Article 14 and 21
relevance: Struck down the twin bail conditions that made bail nearly impossible under PMLA

case_name: Shayara Bano vs. Union of India
core_issue: Constitutional validity of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat)
holding: Instant triple talaq is unconstitutional as it violates Article 14 and is not essential to Islamic practice
principles_established: Triple talaq is not an essential religious practice under Islam
Practice violates the fundamental right to equality
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 subsequently enacted
relevance: Outlawed the practice of instant divorce among Indian Muslims and strengthened gender justice

case_name: Seema Ghosh vs. State of Rajasthan
core_issue: Compulsory registration of marriages
holding: Registration of marriages should be made compulsory regardless of religion
principles_established: Marriage registration is compulsory in the interest of women
Prevents denial of marriage, bigamy and abandonment
Directs states to frame rules for compulsory registration
relevance: Led to nationwide push for mandatory marriage registration to protect women's rights

case_name: Danial Latifi vs. Union of India
core_issue: Muslim women's right to maintenance after divorce under Article 21
holding: Section 125 CrPC applies to Muslim women even after divorce; maintenance must be paid for entire life or until remarriage
acts_affected: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
principles_established: Muslim divorced women are entitled to maintenance under Sec. 125 CrPC
Maintenance under Muslim Women Act must be fair and reasonable
Obligation of husband continues until wife remarries
relevance: Upheld maintenance rights of Muslim divorced women while protecting personal law

case_name: Githa Hariharan vs. Reserve Bank of India
core_issue: Whether mother can be natural guardian of a child during father's lifetime
holding: Mother is a natural guardian under Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act even during father's lifetime if father is absent or uninterested
acts_affected: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Sec. 6
principles_established: Mother's right as natural guardian is not subordinate to father
Guardianship laws must be interpreted in light of gender equality
Father's 'after' in Sec. 6 does not mean mother is disqualifed
relevance: Advanced gender equality in guardianship rights; mother recognized as equal guardian

case_name: Vishaka vs. State of Rajasthan
core_issue: Sexual harassment of women at workplace
holding: Laid down guidelines (Vishaka Guidelines) to prevent sexual harassment at workplace until legislation is enacted
principles_established: Sexual harassment violates fundamental rights to equality and life
Employers must provide safe working environment
Complaints committee must be constituted in every workplace
Legislation later enacted as POSH Act, 2013
relevance: Established landmark framework against workplace sexual harassment; precursor to POSH Act, 2013

case_name: M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India
core_issue: Strict and absolute liability for hazardous industries
holding: Established the principle of absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous activities; liability is not subject to exceptions under strict liability
principles_established: Absolute liability for harm from hazardous substances
No exceptions to liability (no act of God, third party, etc.)
Quantum of damages must be proportional to enterprise's capacity
relevance: Created strict environmental liability standard far exceeding the English rule in Rylands vs. Fletcher

case_name: Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha
core_issue: Whether medical services are covered under the Consumer Protection Act
holding: Medical services rendered by doctors and hospitals are 'services' under the Consumer Protection Act and medical negligence is actionable
principles_established: Medical services fall within ambit of consumer law
Free services in government hospitals may be exempt
Paid medical services are subject to consumer protection
relevance: Brought medical profession under consumer law, making doctors accountable for negligence

case_name: Delhi Transport Corporation vs. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress
core_issue: Right to livelihood and arbitrary termination of workers
holding: Right to livelihood is part of Article 21; termination without notice and without reasons violates natural justice and fundamental rights
principles_established: Right to livelihood flows from Article 21
Termination must be by reasoned order and after hearing
Unregulated power to terminate is arbitrary under Article 14
relevance: Expanded labour protections by linking employment security to fundamental rights

case_name: LIC of India vs. Consumer Education & Research Centre
core_issue: Insurance contracts, public duty and fundamental rights
holding: Insurance contracts are imbued with public duty; LIC as state must act fairly and all citizens have right to insurance coverage without discrimination
principles_established: Right to life includes right to livelihood and health
Insurance is a social security measure
State instrumentalities cannot discriminate in insurance coverage
relevance: Held that insurance companies have a public duty and cannot arbitrarily deny coverage

case_name: State of Rajasthan vs. Balchand
core_issue: Bail jurisprudence — rule vs. exception
holding: Bail is the rule and jail is the exception; personal liberty is paramount and should not be curtailed except in compelling circumstances
principles_established: Bail is a rule, jail is an exception
Personal liberty under Article 21 is supreme
Pre-trial detention should be minimal
relevance: Established the foundational principle of Indian bail jurisprudence

case_name: Sanjay Chandra vs. Central Bureau of Investigation
core_issue: Bail in economic offences — 2G spectrum case
holding: Seriousness of allegation and economic offence character alone are not grounds to deny bail; gravity of punishment is not the same as gravity of offence for bail purpose
principles_established: Economic offences do not automatically disentitle bail
Pre-trial detention cannot be punitive
Liberty of accused is relevant even in serious economic crimes
relevance: Established that economic offences do not create a separate, stricter bail regime

case_name: Satender Kumar Antil vs. Central Bureau of Investigation
core_issue: Comprehensive bail guidelines under criminal law
holding: Laid down comprehensive guidelines to ensure bail is granted liberally; no arrest for trivial reasons and strict compliance with Sections 41, 41A CrPC
principles_established: Categories of offences for bail purposes
Directions to magistrates to apply bail provisions liberally
Strict compliance with notice provisions under 41A
Consequences of illegal arrests and non-compliance
relevance: Comprehensive modern framework to decongest prisons by liberalizing bail

case_name: Arnab Goswami vs. State of Maharashtra
core_issue: Bail and personal liberty in cases involving serious allegations
holding: Personal liberty cannot be curtailed even where allegations are serious; courts must not treat bail as a punishment
principles_established: Personal liberty is paramount even in serious cases
Bail cannot be denied as a punishment
Length of incarceration is relevant for bail consideration
relevance: Reinforced that personal liberty under Article 21 is not forfeited by serious allegations alone

case_name: Union of India vs. K.A. Najeeb
core_issue: Bail under UAPA — right to speedy trial
holding: Right to speedy trial under Article 21 applies even under special acts like UAPA; courts can grant bail if trial is delayed despite stringent bail conditions in the Act
principles_established: Right to speedy trial overrides restrictive bail provisions
Stringent bail conditions in UAPA are not absolute
Prolonged incarceration without trial violates Article 21
relevance: Broke the nearly absolute bar on bail under UAPA by invoking fundamental rights
